# Solution

## Setup and Reduction to i.i.d. Variables

By the independent increments property of Brownian motion, the process $\{B_t - B_{n-1} : n-1 \le t \le n\}$ is a standard Brownian motion on $[0,1]$, independent of $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$. Therefore the random variables

$$M_n = \max_{n-1 \le t \le n} |B_t - B_{n-1}|$$

are **i.i.d.**, each with the same distribution as $X := \max_{0 \le s \le 1} |B_s|$.

The problem reduces to: find the threshold $r > 0$ such that $P\!\big(X_n \le r\sqrt{\log n}\ \text{for all sufficiently large } n\big) = 1$, where $\{X_n\}$ are i.i.d. copies of $X$.

## Tail Estimate for $X = \max_{0 \le s \le 1} |B_s|$

By the reflection principle:
$$P\!\Big(\sup_{0 \le s \le 1} B_s \ge a\Big) = 2\,P(B_1 \ge a) = 2\big(1 - \Phi(a)\big),$$
and similarly $P\!\big(\inf_{0 \le s \le 1} B_s \le -a\big) = 2\big(1-\Phi(a)\big)$.

By inclusion–exclusion:
$$P(X \ge a) = 4\big(1-\Phi(a)\big) - P\!\Big(\sup_{0\le s\le 1} B_s \ge a,\ \inf_{0\le s\le 1} B_s \le -a\Big).$$

For large $a$, the joint event (hitting both $+a$ and $-a$ within $[0,1]$) is of strictly smaller order than $1-\Phi(a)$, so:

$$P(X \ge a) \sim \frac{4}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\frac{e^{-a^2/2}}{a} \quad \text{as } a \to \infty.$$

In particular, the **exponential rate** is $e^{-a^2/2}$, which is what governs the Borel–Cantelli threshold.

## Borel–Cantelli Analysis

Set $a_n = r\sqrt{\log n}$. Then:

$$P\!\big(X_n > r\sqrt{\log n}\big) \sim \frac{4}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\frac{e^{-r^2 \log n / 2}}{r\sqrt{\log n}} = \frac{4}{r\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\frac{n^{-r^2/2}}{\sqrt{\log n}}.$$

**Convergence of the series** $\sum_n P(X_n > r\sqrt{\log n})$:

$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{n^{-r^2/2}}{\sqrt{\log n}} \quad \text{converges} \iff r^2/2 > 1 \iff r > \sqrt{2}.$$

At the boundary $r = \sqrt{2}$: $\sum \frac{1}{n\sqrt{\log n}} = \infty$ (by the integral test, $\int_2^\infty \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{\log x}} = 2\sqrt{\log x}\,\Big|_2^\infty = \infty$).

**Case $r > \sqrt{2}$:** The series converges. By the **first Borel–Cantelli lemma**,
$$P\!\big(X_n > r\sqrt{\log n}\ \text{i.o.}\big) = 0,$$
so $X_n \le r\sqrt{\log n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$, almost surely. ✓

**Case $r \le \sqrt{2}$:** The series diverges. Since $\{X_n\}$ are **independent**, the **second Borel–Cantelli lemma** gives
$$P\!\big(X_n > r\sqrt{\log n}\ \text{i.o.}\big) = 1,$$
so $X_n > r\sqrt{\log n}$ infinitely often, almost surely. ✗

## Conclusion

The property "$M_n \le r\sqrt{\log n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$, a.s." holds if and only if $r > \sqrt{2}$. The **critical threshold value** is:

$$\boxed{r = \sqrt{2}}.$$

This is the exact boundary: for any $r > \sqrt{2}$ the inequality holds eventually a.s., while for $r \le \sqrt{2}$ it fails infinitely often a.s.

### PROOF COMPLETE
